reference.title: Side Crunch
reference.listing: Video; data sheet: body part Waist, equipment Body weight, exercise type Strength

breathing.pattern: Exhale as you lift the shoulders, inhale as you lower.
breathing.cadence: About 1 s up, a short squeeze, about 1.8 s down

prescription.tempo: About 1 s up, brief pause, 2 s down
prescription.progression: Slower lowering and a 2 s hold, then the feet anchored (larger range) or a side plank

cues.text: Lie on your left side, hips stacked, knees slightly bent, top leg resting on the bottom one. Top fingertips behind the head, elbow wide; bottom hand resting on the mat in front of the chest.
Breathe out and side-bend to lift both shoulders off the mat, bringing the top ribs toward the top hip.
Short squeeze at the top; stay on your side, chest facing forward, not rolling onto the back.
Breathe in and lower slowly until the bottom shoulder touches down.
Rest briefly; finish the set, then switch to the other side.

mistakes.mistake: Rolling back onto the shoulder blades
mistakes.fix: Keep the hips stacked and the chest facing forward.

mistakes.mistake: Pushing up with the bottom hand or pulling the head
mistakes.fix: The bottom hand only balances; the top ribs lead the lift.

mistakes.mistake: Swinging the legs to get up
mistakes.fix: Legs stay heavy on the mat; reduce the range.

kinematics.norm: Small range: the shoulders lift a few centimetres to a hand width (clinical opinion)
Bottom shoulder clears the mat (clinical opinion)
Hips stacked, knees slightly bent, legs still (clinical opinion)
Top hand supports the head; the bottom hand only balances (clinical opinion)
About 1 s up and 2 s down (clinical opinion)

sources.title: Konrad, Schmitz and Denner 2001, neuromuscular evaluation of trunk-training exercises (J Athl Train 36(2):109-118; PMC155519)
Escamilla, Lewis, Pecson, Imamura and Andrews 2016, muscle activation among supine, prone and side position exercises with and without a Swiss ball (Sports Health 8(4):372-379; PMC4922527)
McGill, Juker and Kropf, quantitative intramuscular myoelectric activity of quadratus lumborum during a wide variety of tasks (Clinical Biomechanics)

cautions: Stop if you feel sharp, radiating or nerve-type pain.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
Low-back pain with side bending: keep the range small or use a side plank on the knees instead (clinical opinion).
Shoulder pain lying on the side: put a folded towel under the bottom shoulder or keep the bottom arm along the floor.
Pregnancy and postpartum (diastasis recti): get individual guidance before dynamic trunk-flexion work.
The athlete mesh rests on the mat; the rig collision shapes are thicker than the mesh at the back and buttocks, so floorTolerance records how far those proxy shapes sink below the mat surface.
modify: Bottom arm along the floor or across the chest if the bottom shoulder is uncomfortable.
Feet anchored under a support for a bigger range (harder).
progressions: Slow 3 s lowering with a 2 s hold.

muscleNotes.obliques_r: The top-side external and internal obliques bend the trunk sideways against gravity: side-lying lateral flexion with fixed legs gave about 98% MVC external oblique in Konrad 2001, and a side crunch on a Swiss ball about 50% MVIC external oblique (Escamilla 2016).
muscleNotes.obliques_l: The top-side external and internal obliques bend the trunk sideways against gravity: side-lying lateral flexion with fixed legs gave about 98% MVC external oblique in Konrad 2001, and a side crunch on a Swiss ball about 50% MVIC external oblique (Escamilla 2016).
muscleNotes.core: Rectus abdominis assists a little (about 21% MVIC upper rectus in the ball side crunch, Escamilla 2016).
muscleNotes.spinal_extensors_r: Quadratus lumborum and the erector spinae on the top side help side-bend and keep the trunk from rolling; quadratus lumborum is a strong lateral stabiliser (McGill, Juker and Kropf).
muscleNotes.spinal_extensors_l: Quadratus lumborum and the erector spinae on the top side help side-bend and keep the trunk from rolling; quadratus lumborum is a strong lateral stabiliser (McGill, Juker and Kropf).
muscleNotes.glute_med_r: Holds the top hip steady so the pelvis does not roll back (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.glute_med_l: Holds the top hip steady so the pelvis does not roll back (clinical opinion).
